title: The body: the charnel ground
hookLine: a body one day dead, two days, three; this body too is of that nature (MN 10), offered gently

cards: A quick word before today. The last body exercise in the sutta is about death, and it's direct.
If you're grieving right now, or today just isn't the day, it's completely fine to listen lightly, or to spend the practice with your breath instead. Nothing is lost.
For everyone else: it's easy to live as if one's own body were the one exception. Other people get old. Other people die.
Somehow, not quite me. The sutta asks for a gentle, honest look at that.

teach.b: In the sutta's world, a charnel ground is a place where bodies were left out in the open, and the texts picture monks going there to practice.
The sutta describes a practitioner who sees a body there: one day dead, two days, three.
Then, over nine stages, it follows what happens next, until only scattered bones remain, bleached white, and finally bones crumbled to dust.
At each stage the practitioner turns to their own body and reflects: this body too is of the same nature. It will become like that.
It is not exempt. The whole exercise rests on that line: this body too. It sounds grim, but look at what it's for.
It isn't meant to frighten, or to make life feel worthless.
In Buddhist teaching, remembering death, maranasati, is meant to wake you up to what matters. The Buddha is remembered as saying that mindfulness of death, well practiced, is of great fruit.
If this body won't last forever, a postponed phone call matters. An old grudge weighs more than it's worth. And an ordinary morning is precious, exactly because it's passing.
Some practitioners say this reflection, done gently, leaves them calmer, not sadder. And the chorus comes back even here: arising and passing away, in the body itself.

how: Reflection on death (maranasati) is practiced in many Buddhist traditions; some monastics use a skeleton or images of the stages, and lay practitioners often reflect quietly that this body, too, will not last.

seeing that this body, too, will pass away

games.q: match each piece of the charnel ground section.
p: where bodies were left outside town
from one day dead to dust

s: the charnel ground practice is meant to make life feel worthless
it's meant to wake you up to what matters, because life is passing.
the sutta describes nine stages, ending with bones crumbled to dust
at each stage the practitioner reflects: this body too.
at each stage, the practitioner turns back to their own body
this body too is of the same nature; it is not exempt.

games.q: you're a monk at the charnel ground, looking at a body three days dead. what does the sutta ask you to do next?
o: look away and think of something pleasant.
turn to your own body: this too is of the same nature.
pray for the dead person's rebirth.
games.why: at every stage the practitioner applies what they see to their own body: it will become like that; it is not exempt.

practice: Feel your body breathing, alive, warm, working, and quietly, if it feels right, reflect: this body too will not last forever.
Let the thought be soft, not frightening, then ask one question, given that, what matters today, and let an answer come, or not. If this feels too heavy right now, just rest with the breath instead.

wordCard.voice: The body, the charnel ground. Seeing another body return to dust, the practitioner reflects: this body too is of that nature.

carryVoice: Your line: this body too. Not to frighten, but to show what matters. Day two hundred fifty-five, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the nine charnel-ground contemplations
